========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, hello, doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I... well, I came because I am just losing so much of my time lately, and it's becoming quite exhausting at my age. You see, over the years—I'm 86 now—you accumulate a lot of history. And I have always been very organized, I used to manage all our household accounts and keep everything very meticulous... but lately, I spend far, far too much of my day just... opening things. 

The same folders, the same heavy desk drawers, these little labeled archival boxes I keep in the spare room... I just open them again and again and again. I have to make sure that all the important papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them. I'm talking about birth certificates, the deed to the house, my late husband's letters, the grandchildren's baptism records... I just get this terrible, nagging feeling that they've gone missing or I've misplaced them somehow. 

And the most frustrating part of it all is that I will check a box, see that the papers are perfectly safe right where they belong, close the lid, walk out into the hallway... and then just a few minutes later, I have to turn right back around and open that exact same box to check it again. Sometimes I haven't even made it to the kitchen to put the kettle on before I'm back in there pulling out the same manila folder. It just eats up my whole afternoon, just opening and checking, over and over, even though I know I *just* looked at it. It's just very hard on my knees, getting up and down like that all day, but I simply can't seem to stop myself from going back to make sure...

Oh, heavens, yes. It's... it's really a dreadful feeling. Just a terrible, tight knot right here in my chest. I will be sitting in my armchair—the blue one by the window where I like to read the morning paper—and I'll try to just relax, maybe watch a bit of television or do some knitting, but my mind just won't let me be. 

Even when I know better, even when I *just* looked and I know everything is fine, this... this thought will just start needling me. It just pokes and pokes at my brain. I'll suddenly think, "What if I accidentally threw away Arthur's old tax papers?" Or, "What if I was tidying up and I put my mother's pound cake recipe in the wrong box?" And I know it sounds silly to worry about old taxes—Arthur has been gone for nearly a decade now, bless him, and heaven knows the government doesn't care about our filings from 1998 anymore—but I just can't seem to let the thought pass. 

If I try to just sit there and ignore it, the worry just grows and grows until I feel like I've done something terribly, terribly careless. I start imagining that the recipe is lost forever, or that I've ruined our family records, and the feeling is just so intensely distressing. Because I have prided myself on my organization since I was a young woman doing my bachelor's degree, you know? I kept all my university notes perfectly filed, I never lost a single syllabus. So the very idea of being that careless now, in my old age, it just eats away at me. It makes my heart race and my stomach churn until I simply have to get up from my chair, walk all the way back down the hall, and go look again, just to prove to myself that I haven't ruined everything...

Oh, no, no... not at a specific time. I honestly wish it were just at a specific time, like how I used to balance the checkbook every Sunday evening right after dinner. Arthur would wash the dishes and I would sit at the dining room table with my ledger and my reading glasses. There's no schedule to it at all, which is precisely why it eats up my whole day. 

And as for *how* I check... well, I don't think I do it in any special way. I don't have a particular sequence or anything like that. I just... I just have to open the box or the drawer, you see. I just go straight for whatever it is I'm worried about in that moment. If my mind suddenly says, "Where is the deed to the house?" then I just go straight for the heavy bottom drawer and find the red folder. I pull it out, I look at the paper, sometimes I just touch the edge of it just to feel that it's real and it's right there where I left it. But I don't have a... a routine, or a special order I go through. It's really just a desperate scramble to find the exact item my brain is telling me I've ruined or lost. 

I just look at it, tell myself, "See, you silly old woman, it's perfectly fine," and put it back. But then, as I said, ten minutes later I might be right back in there doing the exact same thing because the feeling returned. It's just so terribly random, doctor, and I think that's why it exhausts me so much. You just never know when the worry is going to strike next...

Oh, no, dear, nothing like that. I don't have a specific phrase or... or a little poem I recite to myself, if that's what you mean. Oh, it most certainly has, and that... that might be the most heartbreaking part of it all. It really is. You see, I used to be quite the social butterfly, even in my old age. I was too embarrassed to have anyone over. How could I let my friends see me living like that? If it were just like that, an appointment I could keep with myself, it wouldn't be quite so bothersome. \n\nBut no, it's... it's completely unpredictable. It happens whenever that dreadful thought decides to pop into my head. It could be first thing in the morning when I'm just trying to enjoy my toast and marmalade, or it could be right in the middle of the afternoon when I'm waiting for the postman. There's no schedule to it at all, which is precisely why it eats up my whole day. \n\nAnd as for *how* I check... well, I don't think I do it in any special way. I don't have a particular sequence or anything like that. I just... I just have to open the box or the drawer, you see. I just go straight for whatever it is I'm worried about in that moment. If my mind suddenly says, \"Where is the deed to the house?\" then I just go straight for the heavy bottom drawer and find the red folder. I pull it out, I look at the paper, sometimes I just touch the edge of it just to feel that it's real and it's right there where I left it. But I don't have a... a routine, or a special order I go through. It's really just a desperate scramble to find the exact item my brain is telling me I've ruined or lost. \n\nI just look at it, tell myself, \"See, you silly old woman, it's perfectly fine,\" and put it back. But then, as I said, ten minutes later I might be right back in there doing the exact same thing because the feeling returned. It's just so terribly random, doctor, and I think that's why it exhausts me so much. You just never know when the worry is going to strike next...\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have to think about these papers and keepsakes in a certain way, or repeat certain thoughts in your head, when you're checking on them?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, dear, nothing like that. I don't have a specific phrase or... or a little poem I recite to myself, if that's what you mean. I know some people do that sort of thing—my sister Margaret, rest her soul, used to always hum a little tune when she was nervous, just the same three notes over and over. But no, I don't do anything of that sort. \n\nWhen I'm looking at the papers, my mind is really just focused on the item itself. I'm just looking at it, perhaps reading the top line—like the header on the deed, or the date on one of Arthur's letters—just to be absolutely certain it's the right piece of paper. I suppose I do sometimes say things out loud to myself, like I mentioned before, just scolding myself a bit. \"See here, it's right where you left it,\" or \"Everything is perfectly fine.\" But it's not a... a ritualized thought, or a specific sentence I *have* to think in order to feel better. \n\nIt's really just the visual confirmation I need. Just seeing it there in its proper place. Though, as I say that, I suppose the relief doesn't last very long anyway, does it? Because even after I see it, and even after I tell myself it's fine, my brain just resets and the worry starts all over again. But no, to answer your question, there are no special thoughts or repeated phrases I have to use. Just the looking. Just the endless, exhausting looking...\n\nDoctor: Has this behavior of constantly checking papers and keepsakes affected your relationships with family or friends, or impacted your ability to do things you enjoy?\n\nPatient: Oh, it most certainly has, and that... that might be the most heartbreaking part of it all. It really is. You see, I used to be quite the social butterfly, even in my old age. I've always loved having people over. Arthur and I used to host dinner parties every other Friday, and I've tried to keep that spirit of hospitality alive, I really have. \n\nBut lately... oh, it's just become impossible. Just last week, I was supposed to have my mentoring session—I volunteer to help young university girls with their English literature coursework, you know, since I have my degree and I just love the classics so much. We were supposed to read through some of George Eliot's letters. I had the tea service all set out, the good silver polished, and then... well, then I thought about the box of Arthur's old tax returns in the hall closet. I just had to check them. And then I had to check my mother's recipes. And before I knew it, I had pulled half the boxes out of the closet, papers were everywhere, and I had completely lost track of time. \n\nI lost the entire afternoon, doctor. Just gone. The young girl rang the bell, and I... I couldn't even answer the door. I just stood there in the hallway, surrounded by all these piles of paper, feeling so utterly ashamed. I had to call her later and make up a story about feeling under the weather, which I hate doing, because I pride myself on being honest. \n\nAnd it's not just the mentoring. I've been skipping my Wednesday afternoon book club, too. The ladies always take turns hosting, and it was supposed to be my turn last month. We were reading a lovely biography of Queen Victoria. But my apartment was just in such a state of disarray from all my checking and digging through drawers. I was too embarrassed to have anyone over. How could I let my friends see me living like that? With folders and keepsakes strewn across the dining table where we were meant to have our cucumber sandwiches? So I cancelled. I just... I isolate myself because I can't control it, and I don't want anyone to see what a foolish, disorganized mess I've become. It's terribly lonely, to be quite honest with you.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, doctor, that's exactly what I was just touching on a moment ago with the young girls I mentor and my dear book club ladies. I suppose, when I really sit and think about it, I haven't just missed a session here or there—I really have had to stop doing them altogether at this point. It breaks my heart to admit it out loud, it truly does, because those were the things that gave my week structure. 

But it's just as I was saying... I lose whole afternoons to this. Entire days, just swallowed up. I'll start right after my lunchtime tea, thinking I'll just take a quick peek at the insurance papers just to settle my mind, and the next thing I know, the grandfather clock in the hall is chiming five o'clock and the sun is starting to set. 

And the aftermath... oh, the aftermath is why I've had to just cancel everything entirely. Because I've spent all those hours pulling things out of the closets and the drawers, my apartment is left in such a terrible state of disarray. It looks like a burglar has ransacked the place, truly it does! I'll have piles of manila folders on the good upholstery, keepsakes scattered all across the dining table where we ought to be sitting with our teacups... I just feel so profoundly embarrassed by it all. I can't possibly let anyone see how I'm living right now. 

So, rather than face the humiliation of having someone knock on the door while my home is in such a chaotic state, I just cancel. I've cancelled so many mentoring sessions now that the university probably won't send me any more students, and I've skipped so many book club meetings I wouldn't be surprised if the ladies think I've moved away. I just keep telling myself I'll get the place tidied up for next week, but then the worry strikes again, the papers come back out, and I'm right back where I started. So, yes, I've had to just stop having anyone over altogether because the shame of them seeing the disarray is simply too much for me to bear.

Oh, well, that's... that's a very thoughtful question, doctor. A very astute question, really, because it's something I've spent a great deal of time pondering myself, usually in the middle of the night when I can't sleep. You know, when you reach my age—eighty-six, though I hardly feel it most days, except perhaps in my knees when it rains—you do start to wonder about these things. You hear so many stories about people losing their faculties, and of course, it's a terrifying prospect. My friend Eleanor, well, she started forgetting her own grandchildren's names, and it was just tragic to watch. 

But for me... no, I don't honestly believe it's my memory failing. I really don't. Because, you see, I know exactly where the things are. I know the deed to the house is in the blue folder in the third drawer down in the study. I know Arthur's letters are in the cedar box on the top shelf of the hall closet. If you were to ask me right now to draw you a map of where every important document in my home is located, I could do it with absolute precision. My memory, thank the Lord, is still quite sharp. I can still quote long passages of Wordsworth and Tennyson from my university days, you know! 

So, no, it's not that I've forgotten where I put them. It's... it's exactly what you said, it's the worry. It's this awful, nagging feeling that somehow, against all logic and reason, the papers might have moved. Or that someone might have come in and taken them, even though my doors are always locked. Or that I might have accidentally thrown them out with the Tuesday rubbish, even though I know perfectly well I haven't been near the filing cabinet. It's the doubt, doctor. It's not a gap in my memory, it's a... a gap in my certainty, if that makes any sense at all. I can picture the papers in the drawer perfectly in my mind's eye, but the picture just isn't enough to satisfy the worry. I have to go and look with my own two eyes, just to prove to that anxious part of my brain that my memory is correct. So, yes, I'm quite certain my memory is fine. It's just the worry that's playing these cruel tricks on me.

Because I've spent all those hours pulling things out of the closets and the drawers, my apartment is left in such a terrible state of disarray. It looks like a burglar has ransacked the place, truly it does! I'll have piles of manila folders on the good upholstery, keepsakes scattered all across the dining table where we ought to be sitting with our teacups... I just feel so profoundly embarrassed by it all. I can't possibly let anyone see how I'm living right now. \n\nSo, rather than face the humiliation of having someone knock on the door while my home is in such a chaotic state, I just cancel. I've cancelled so many mentoring sessions now that the university probably won't send me any more students, and I've skipped so many book club meetings I wouldn't be surprised if the ladies think I've moved away. I just keep telling myself I'll get the place tidied up for next week, but then the worry strikes again, the papers come back out, and I'm right back where I started. So, yes, I've had to just stop having anyone over altogether because the shame of them seeing the disarray is simply too much for me to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your memory is worsening with age, or is it just the worry that's making you feel like you can't remember where things are?\n\nPatient: Oh, well, that's... that's a very thoughtful question, doctor. A very astute question, really, because it's something I've spent a great deal of time pondering myself, usually in the middle of the night when I can't sleep. You know, when you reach my age—eighty-six, though I hardly feel it most days, except perhaps in my knees when it rains—you do start to wonder about these things. You hear so many stories about people losing their faculties, and of course, it's a terrifying prospect. My friend Eleanor, well, she started forgetting her own grandchildren's names, and it was just tragic to watch. \n\nBut for me... no, I don't honestly believe it's my memory failing. I really don't. Because, you see, I know exactly where the things are. I know the deed to the house is in the blue folder in the third drawer down in the study. I know Arthur's letters are in the cedar box on the top shelf of the hall closet. If you were to ask me right now to draw you a map of where every important document in my home is located, I could do it with absolute precision. My memory, thank the Lord, is still quite sharp. I can still quote long passages of Wordsworth and Tennyson from my university days, you know! \n\nSo, no, it's not that I've forgotten where I put them. It's... it's exactly what you said, it's the worry. It's this awful, nagging feeling that somehow, against all logic and reason, the papers might have moved. Or that someone might have come in and taken them, even though my doors are always locked. Or that I might have accidentally thrown them out with the Tuesday rubbish, even though I know perfectly well I haven't been near the filing cabinet. It's the doubt, doctor. I can picture the papers in the drawer perfectly in my mind's eye, but the picture just isn't enough to satisfy the worry. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, goodness me, no. No, not at all. In fact, if you were to walk into my sitting room right this very minute, you would probably chuckle at the very idea of me needing things in any sort of particular order! As I was saying before about the book club ladies and the terrible state of my apartment, things are just piled up willy-nilly everywhere you look these days. 

I really don't mind a bit of clutter, and I certainly don't need things lined up perfectly or arranged in any special way to feel at peace. My late husband, Arthur, well, he was a bit of a stickler for that sort of thing. He used to align his fountain pens on his desk blotter so they were perfectly parallel, bless his heart. He couldn't stand a crooked picture frame. But me? No, I've never been fussy like that. 

When I get that awful urge to check the documents, I just pull them out of the boxes and folders, and once I've laid eyes on them and satisfied that terrible worry, I just set them down wherever there's an empty spot. On the floral sofa, on the tea trolley, right on top of the radiator cover if I'm standing in the hallway! I don't care if the edges of the papers match up or if the folders are color-coded. If I actually needed things to be neat and orderly to feel comfortable, I suppose I'd be in a constant state of agony just looking at the aftermath of my own rummaging. 

So, no, doctor, it's definitely not the arrangement that matters to me. It's just the knowing. I just need to know the items are *there*, safe and sound, even if they're left in a completely disorganized heap on the rug.

Just the endless, exhausting looking...\n\nDoctor: Has this behavior of constantly checking papers and keepsakes affected your relationships with family or friends, or impacted your ability to do things you enjoy?\n\nPatient: Oh, it most certainly has, and that... that might be the most heartbreaking part of it all. Oh, preventing something bad... well, I suppose the "bad thing" is really just that awful, sinking feeling that they're gone. It's not that I think the house will catch fire or... or that the sky will fall, nothing quite so dramatic as that. It's just the unbearable thought of losing them.

It isn't just a matter of checking the locks before bed like a normal person might do. I will find myself opening the exact same folders, the same heavy oak drawers in the study, those little labeled boxes I keep on the top shelf of the closet... I open them again and again and again. Just to make absolutely sure the important papers and my precious keepsakes are right where I left them. 

And the truly absurd part, doctor—the part that is so terribly exhausting and makes me feel so foolish—is that I will do this even when I just checked them a few minutes before! I will literally look inside a labeled box, see Arthur's letters, close the lid, walk into the kitchen to put the kettle on for my afternoon tea, and before the water even begins to simmer... there it is. That dreadful whisper of doubt. "Did I really see them?" "What if one slipped out the back of the folder?" "What if I imagined it?" 

And so I have to turn right back around, leave the kettle on the stove, and go open that very same drawer and that very same box all over again. I just can't seem to hold onto the certainty for more than a few minutes at a time. It's a relentless cycle, just opening and reopening, looking at the same keepsakes, the same documents, all day long.

Sometimes I haven't even made it to the kitchen to put the kettle on before I'm back in there pulling out the same manila folder. It just eats up my whole afternoon, just opening and checking, over and over, even though I know I *just* looked at it. It's just very hard on my knees, getting up and down like that all day, but I simply can't seem to stop myself from going back to make sure...\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or worried when you're not checking these papers and keepsakes?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens, yes. It's... it's really a dreadful feeling. Just a terrible, tight knot right here in my chest. I will be sitting in my armchair—the blue one by the window where I like to read the morning paper—and I'll try to just relax, maybe watch a bit of television or do some knitting, but my mind just won't let me be. \n\nEven when I know better, even when I *just* looked and I know everything is fine, this... this thought will just start needling me. It just pokes and pokes at my brain. I'll suddenly think, \"What if I accidentally threw away Arthur's old tax papers?\" Or, \"What if I was tidying up and I put my mother's pound cake recipe in the wrong box?\" And I know it sounds silly to worry about old taxes—Arthur has been gone for nearly a decade now, bless him, and heaven knows the government doesn't care about our filings from 1998 anymore—but I just can't seem to let the thought pass. \n\nIf I try to just sit there and ignore it, the worry just grows and grows until I feel like I've done something terribly, terribly careless. I start imagining that the recipe is lost forever, or that I've ruined our family records, and the feeling is just so intensely distressing. Because I have prided myself on my organization since I was a young woman doing my bachelor's degree, you know? I kept all my university notes perfectly filed, I never lost a single syllabus. So the very idea of being that careless now, in my old age, it just eats away at me. It makes my heart race and my stomach churn until I simply have to get up from my chair, walk all the way back down the hall, and go look again, just to prove to myself that I haven't ruined everything...\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have to check these papers and keepsakes in a specific way or at a specific time?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no... not at a specific time. I honestly wish it were just at a specific time, like how I used to balance the checkbook every Sunday evening right after dinner. Arthur would wash the dishes and I would sit at the dining room table with my ledger and my reading glasses. If it were just like that, an appointment I could keep with myself, it wouldn't be quite so bothersome. \n\nBut no, it's... it's completely unpredictable. It happens whenever that dreadful thought decides to pop into my head. It could be first thing in the morning when I'm just trying to enjoy my toast and marmalade, or it could be right in the middle of the afternoon when I'm waiting for the postman. There's no schedule to it at all, which is precisely why it eats up my whole day. \n\nAnd as for *how* I check... well, I don't think I do it in any special way. I don't have a particular sequence or anything like that. I just... I just have to open the box or the drawer, you see. I just go straight for whatever it is I'm worried about in that moment. If my mind suddenly says, \"Where is the deed to the house?\" then I just go straight for the heavy bottom drawer and find the red folder. I pull it out, I look at the paper, sometimes I just touch the edge of it just to feel that it's real and it's right there where I left it. But I don't have a... a routine, or a special order I go through. It's really just a desperate scramble to find the exact item my brain is telling me I've ruined or lost. \n\nI just look at it, tell myself, \"See, you silly old woman, it's perfectly fine,\" and put it back. But then, as I said, ten minutes later I might be right back in there doing the exact same thing because the feeling returned. It's just so terribly random, doctor, and I think that's why it exhausts me so much. You just never know when the worry is going to strike next...\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have to think about these papers and keepsakes in a certain way, or repeat certain thoughts in your head, when you're checking on them?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, dear, nothing like that. I don't have a specific phrase or... or a little poem I recite to myself, if that's what you mean. I know some people do that sort of thing—my sister Margaret, rest her soul, used to always hum a little tune when she was nervous, just the same three notes over and over. But no, I don't do anything of that sort. \n\nWhen I'm looking at the papers, my mind is really just focused on the item itself. I'm just looking at it, perhaps reading the top line—like the header on the deed, or the date on one of Arthur's letters—just to be absolutely certain it's the right piece of paper. I suppose I do sometimes say things out loud to myself, like I mentioned before, just scolding myself a bit. \"See here, it's right where you left it,\" or \"Everything is perfectly fine.\" But it's not a... a ritualized thought, or a specific sentence I *have* to think in order to feel better. \n\nIt's really just the visual confirmation I need. Just seeing it there in its proper place. Though, as I say that, I suppose the relief doesn't last very long anyway, does it? Because even after I see it, and even after I tell myself it's fine, my brain just resets and the worry starts all over again. But no, to answer your question, there are no special thoughts or repeated phrases I have to use. Just the looking. Just the endless, exhausting looking...\n\nDoctor: Has this behavior of constantly checking papers and keepsakes affected your relationships with family or friends, or impacted your ability to do things you enjoy?\n\nPatient: Oh, it most certainly has, and that... that might be the most heartbreaking part of it all. It really is. You see, I used to be quite the social butterfly, even in my old age. I've always loved having people over. Arthur and I used to host dinner parties every other Friday, and I've tried to keep that spirit of hospitality alive, I really have. \n\nBut lately... oh, it's just become impossible. Just last week, I was supposed to have my mentoring session—I volunteer to help young university girls with their English literature coursework, you know, since I have my degree and I just love the classics so much. We were supposed to read through some of George Eliot's letters. I had the tea service all set out, the good silver polished, and then... well, then I thought about the box of Arthur's old tax returns in the hall closet. I just had to check them. And then I had to check my mother's recipes. And before I knew it, I had pulled half the boxes out of the closet, papers were everywhere, and I had completely lost track of time. \n\nI lost the entire afternoon, doctor. Just gone. The young girl rang the bell, and I... I couldn't even answer the door. I just stood there in the hallway, surrounded by all these piles of paper, feeling so utterly ashamed. I had to call her later and make up a story about feeling under the weather, which I hate doing, because I pride myself on being honest. \n\nAnd it's not just the mentoring. I've been skipping my Wednesday afternoon book club, too. The ladies always take turns hosting, and it was supposed to be my turn last month. We were reading a lovely biography of Queen Victoria. But my apartment was just in such a state of disarray from all my checking and digging through drawers. I was too embarrassed to have anyone over. How could I let my friends see me living like that? With folders and keepsakes strewn across the dining table where we were meant to have our cucumber sandwiches? So I cancelled. I just... I isolate myself because I can't control it, and I don't want anyone to see what a foolish, disorganized mess I've become. It's terribly lonely, to be quite honest with you.\n\nDoctor: Are there any daily activities that you've had to stop doing altogether because of this checking behavior?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, doctor, that's exactly what I was just touching on a moment ago with the young girls I mentor and my dear book club ladies. I suppose, when I really sit and think about it, I haven't just missed a session here or there—I really have had to stop doing them altogether at this point. It breaks my heart to admit it out loud, it truly does, because those were the things that gave my week structure. \n\nBut it's just as I was saying... I lose whole afternoons to this. Entire days, just swallowed up. I'll start right after my lunchtime tea, thinking I'll just take a quick peek at the insurance papers just to settle my mind, and the next thing I know, the grandfather clock in the hall is chiming five o'clock and the sun is starting to set. \n\nAnd the aftermath... oh, the aftermath is why I've had to just cancel everything entirely. Because I've spent all those hours pulling things out of the closets and the drawers, my apartment is left in such a terrible state of disarray. It looks like a burglar has ransacked the place, truly it does! I'll have piles of manila folders on the good upholstery, keepsakes scattered all across the dining table where we ought to be sitting with our teacups... I just feel so profoundly embarrassed by it all. I can't possibly let anyone see how I'm living right now. \n\nSo, rather than face the humiliation of having someone knock on the door while my home is in such a chaotic state, I just cancel. I've cancelled so many mentoring sessions now that the university probably won't send me any more students, and I've skipped so many book club meetings I wouldn't be surprised if the ladies think I've moved away. I just keep telling myself I'll get the place tidied up for next week, but then the worry strikes again, the papers come back out, and I'm right back where I started. So, yes, I've had to just stop having anyone over altogether because the shame of them seeing the disarray is simply too much for me to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your memory is worsening with age, or is it just the worry that's making you feel like you can't remember where things are?\n\nPatient: Oh, well, that's... that's a very thoughtful question, doctor. A very astute question, really, because it's something I've spent a great deal of time pondering myself, usually in the middle of the night when I can't sleep. You know, when you reach my age—eighty-six, though I hardly feel it most days, except perhaps in my knees when it rains—you do start to wonder about these things. You hear so many stories about people losing their faculties, and of course, it's a terrifying prospect. My friend Eleanor, well, she started forgetting her own grandchildren's names, and it was just tragic to watch. \n\nBut for me... no, I don't honestly believe it's my memory failing. I really don't. Because, you see, I know exactly where the things are. I know the deed to the house is in the blue folder in the third drawer down in the study. I know Arthur's letters are in the cedar box on the top shelf of the hall closet. If you were to ask me right now to draw you a map of where every important document in my home is located, I could do it with absolute precision. My memory, thank the Lord, is still quite sharp. I can still quote long passages of Wordsworth and Tennyson from my university days, you know! \n\nSo, no, it's not that I've forgotten where I put them. It's... it's exactly what you said, it's the worry. It's this awful, nagging feeling that somehow, against all logic and reason, the papers might have moved. Or that someone might have come in and taken them, even though my doors are always locked. Or that I might have accidentally thrown them out with the Tuesday rubbish, even though I know perfectly well I haven't been near the filing cabinet. It's the doubt, doctor. It's not a gap in my memory, it's a... a gap in my certainty, if that makes any sense at all. I can picture the papers in the drawer perfectly in my mind's eye, but the picture just isn't enough to satisfy the worry. I have to go and look with my own two eyes, just to prove to that anxious part of my brain that my memory is correct. So, yes, I'm quite certain my memory is fine. It's just the worry that's playing these cruel tricks on me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like things need to be in a certain order or arranged in a specific way for you to feel comfortable?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness me, no. No, not at all. In fact, if you were to walk into my sitting room right this very minute, you would probably chuckle at the very idea of me needing things in any sort of particular order! As I was saying before about the book club ladies and the terrible state of my apartment, things are just piled up willy-nilly everywhere you look these days. \n\nI really don't mind a bit of clutter, and I certainly don't need things lined up perfectly or arranged in any special way to feel at peace. My late husband, Arthur, well, he was a bit of a stickler for that sort of thing. He used to align his fountain pens on his desk blotter so they were perfectly parallel, bless his heart. He couldn't stand a crooked picture frame. But me? No, I've never been fussy like that. \n\nWhen I get that awful urge to check the documents, I just pull them out of the boxes and folders, and once I've laid eyes on them and satisfied that terrible worry, I just set them down wherever there's an empty spot. On the floral sofa, on the tea trolley, right on top of the radiator cover if I'm standing in the hallway! I don't care if the edges of the papers match up or if the folders are color-coded. If I actually needed things to be neat and orderly to feel comfortable, I suppose I'd be in a constant state of agony just looking at the aftermath of my own rummaging. \n\nSo, no, doctor, it's definitely not the arrangement that matters to me. It's just the knowing. I just need to know the items are *there*, safe and sound, even if they're left in a completely disorganized heap on the rug.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like checking these papers and keepsakes helps you prevent something bad from happening?\n\nPatient: Oh, preventing something bad... well, I suppose the \"bad thing\" is really just that awful, sinking feeling that they're gone. It's not that I think the house will catch fire or... or that the sky will fall, nothing quite so dramatic as that. It's just the unbearable thought of losing them. \n\nBut really, it's exactly why I finally realized I had to swallow my pride and come see you. Oh, no, dear, no, not at all. I know I just touched on this a moment ago, but it really bears repeating because it's quite the opposite of how I operate. Symmetrical? Exact? Heavens, no. So, yes, I've had to just stop having anyone over altogether because the shame of them seeing the disarray is simply too much for me to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your memory is worsening with age, or is it just the worry that's making you feel like you can't remember where things are?\n\nPatient: Oh, well, that's... that's a very thoughtful question, doctor. Well, as I was saying just a moment ago, it's not that I think a terrible catastrophe is going to occur. It's not like I believe the house will catch fire or the roof will cave in or... or that someone will break in and steal the silver. It's really nothing like that at all. 

It's more of an internal feeling, a terrible, sinking dread. I suppose the "terrible thing" is just the thought of losing them. I mean, Arthur's letters... they're all I have left of him, really. And the deed to the house, well, that's my security, isn't it? If I didn't check on them, I would just be consumed by this awful, nagging worry that they've somehow disappeared or been misplaced. 

I remember once, oh, it must have been a few months ago, I tried to resist the urge to check. I told myself, "Edith, you just looked at the deed yesterday, it's perfectly fine." And I sat down in my favorite armchair by the window, the one with the floral upholstery, and tried to read a book. But I couldn't focus on a single word! My mind kept drifting back to the study, to that heavy oak drawer. The anxiety just built and built until my heart was racing and my hands were trembling, and I felt like I couldn't even catch my breath. I felt so foolish, but the only way to make that horrible feeling go away was to get up and look. 

So, it's not that I think an external disaster will strike if I don't check. It's just that the anxiety itself becomes so unbearable, so completely overwhelming, that I feel like I'll simply burst if I don't go and lay my eyes on those papers right that very second. It's the only way to find any peace, even if it only lasts for a few minutes before the whole dreadful cycle starts all over again.

I can still quote long passages of Wordsworth and Tennyson from my university days, you know! \n\nSo, no, it's not that I've forgotten where I put them. It's... it's exactly what you said, it's the worry. It's this awful, nagging feeling that somehow, against all logic and reason, the papers might have moved. Or that I might have accidentally thrown them out with the Tuesday rubbish, even though I know perfectly well I haven't been near the filing cabinet. It's the doubt, doctor. Control? Oh, heavens, no. Control... no, that's not it at all. If anything, I feel completely out of control! I mean, think about it, doctor. If I had control, I would simply say, "Edith, the deed is in the blue folder in the oak drawer," and that would be the end of it. I don't decide when I'm going to look at Arthur's letters; the anxiety decides for me. It pulls me away from my tea, it pulls me away from my books. It's like being a puppet on a string, and this awful, nagging worry is the one pulling the strings. 

So, no, checking doesn't give me a sense of control. It just highlights how little control I actually have over my own mind right now. It's terribly embarrassing to admit, especially at my age, when one expects to have a certain mastery over oneself, but the truth is, I feel like I'm completely hostage to these papers and keepsakes. I'm just scrambling to keep up with the demands my own brain is making of me, and it's exhausting, truly exhausting. I don't feel in charge of my life at all anymore.

It's a relentless cycle, just opening and reopening, looking at the same keepsakes, the same documents, all day long.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the papers and keepsakes need to be arranged or placed in a symmetrical or exact manner when you're checking on them?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, dear, no, not at all. I know I just touched on this a moment ago, but it really bears repeating because it's quite the opposite of how I operate. Symmetrical? Exact? Heavens, no. As I was saying about Arthur and his fountain pens—he was the one who needed things just so. I'm just frantic, honestly. I'll pull the blue folder out of the study drawer, flip it open, rifle through the pages just to see the raised seal on the deed—just to know it's there—and then I'll practically toss it onto the armchair. Or the floor! Yes, sometimes right onto the Persian rug. \n\nThere's no arranging, no neat stacks, no making sure the corners match up. If you saw the state of my dining room table right now, you'd think a small hurricane had passed through. There are folders overlapping, papers sticking out at odd angles, some face up, some face down. It's a complete jumble. The relief—that fleeting, tiny bit of relief I get—comes entirely from laying my eyes on the item itself, not from how it's sitting on the table. If I had to worry about making everything symmetrical on top of just finding the wretched things, I think I'd simply lose my mind entirely! So, no, the exact placement doesn't matter a whit to me. It's just the seeing. Just the knowing they haven't vanished into thin air.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like something terrible would happen if you didn't check on these papers and keepsakes?\n\nPatient: Well, as I was saying just a moment ago, it's not that I think a terrible catastrophe is going to occur. It's not like I believe the house will catch fire or the roof will cave in or... or that someone will break in and steal the silver. It's really nothing like that at all. \n\nIt's more of an internal feeling, a terrible, sinking dread. I suppose the \"terrible thing\" is just the thought of losing them. I mean, Arthur's letters... they're all I have left of him, really. And the deed to the house, well, that's my security, isn't it? If I didn't check on them, I would just be consumed by this awful, nagging worry that they've somehow disappeared or been misplaced. \n\nI remember once, oh, it must have been a few months ago, I tried to resist the urge to check. I told myself, \"Edith, you just looked at the deed yesterday, it's perfectly fine.\" And I sat down in my favorite armchair by the window, the one with the floral upholstery, and tried to read a book. But I couldn't focus on a single word! My mind kept drifting back to the study, to that heavy oak drawer. The anxiety just built and built until my heart was racing and my hands were trembling, and I felt like I couldn't even catch my breath. I felt so foolish, but the only way to make that horrible feeling go away was to get up and look. \n\nSo, it's not that I think an external disaster will strike if I don't check. It's just that the anxiety itself becomes so unbearable, so completely overwhelming, that I feel like I'll simply burst if I don't go and lay my eyes on those papers right that very second. It's the only way to find any peace, even if it only lasts for a few minutes before the whole dreadful cycle starts all over again.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like checking these papers and keepsakes gives you a sense of control over your life?\n\nPatient: Control? It's like being a puppet on a string, and this awful, nagging worry is the one pulling the strings. \n\nSo, no, checking doesn't give me a sense of control. I'm just scrambling to keep up with the demands my own brain is making of me, and it's exhausting, truly exhausting. With folders and keepsakes strewn across the dining table where we were meant to have our cucumber sandwiches? So I cancelled. I just... I isolate myself because I can't control it, and I don't want anyone to see what a foolish, disorganized mess I've become. It's terribly lonely, to be quite honest with you.\n\nDoctor: Are there any daily activities that you've had to stop doing altogether because of this checking behavior?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, doctor, that's exactly what I was just touching on a moment ago with the young girls I mentor and my dear book club ladies. I suppose, when I really sit and think about it, I haven't just missed a session here or there—I really have had to stop doing them altogether at this point. It breaks my heart to admit it out loud, it truly does, because those were the things that gave my week structure. \n\nBut it's just as I was saying... I lose whole afternoons to this. Entire days, just swallowed up. I'll start right after my lunchtime tea, thinking I'll just take a quick peek at the insurance papers just to settle my mind, and the next thing I know, the grandfather clock in the hall is chiming five o'clock and the sun is starting to set. \n\nAnd the aftermath... oh, the aftermath is why I've had to just cancel everything entirely. Because I've spent all those hours pulling things out of the closets and the drawers, my apartment is left in such a terrible state of disarray. It looks like a burglar has ransacked the place, truly it does! I'll have piles of manila folders on the good upholstery, keepsakes scattered all across the dining table where we ought to be sitting with our teacups... I just feel so profoundly embarrassed by it all. I can't possibly let anyone see how I'm living right now. \n\nSo, rather than face the humiliation of having someone knock on the door while my home is in such a chaotic state, I just cancel. I've cancelled so many mentoring sessions now that the university probably won't send me any more students, and I've skipped so many book club meetings I wouldn't be surprised if the ladies think I've moved away. I just keep telling myself I'll get the place tidied up for next week, but then the worry strikes again, the papers come back out, and I'm right back where I started. So, yes, I've had to just stop having anyone over altogether because the shame of them seeing the disarray is simply too much for me to bear.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your memory is worsening with age, or is it just the worry that's making you feel like you can't remember where things are?\n\nPatient: Oh, well, that's... that's a very thoughtful question, doctor. A very astute question, really, because it's something I've spent a great deal of time pondering myself, usually in the middle of the night when I can't sleep. You know, when you reach my age—eighty-six, though I hardly feel it most days, except perhaps in my knees when it rains—you do start to wonder about these things. You hear so many stories about people losing their faculties, and of course, it's a terrifying prospect. I can still quote long passages of Wordsworth and Tennyson from my university days, you know! \n\nSo, no, it's not that I've forgotten where I put them. It's... it's exactly what you said, it's the worry. It's this awful, nagging feeling that somehow, against all logic and reason, the papers might have moved. Or that someone might have come in and taken them, even though my doors are always locked. Or that I might have accidentally thrown them out with the Tuesday rubbish, even though I know perfectly well I haven't been near the filing cabinet. It's the doubt, doctor. It's not a gap in my memory, it's a... a gap in my certainty, if that makes any sense at all. I can picture the papers in the drawer perfectly in my mind's eye, but the picture just isn't enough to satisfy the worry. I have to go and look with my own two eyes, just to prove to that anxious part of my brain that my memory is correct. So, yes, I'm quite certain my memory is fine. It's just the worry that's playing these cruel tricks on me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like things need to be in a certain order or arranged in a specific way for you to feel comfortable?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness me, no. No, not at all. In fact, if you were to walk into my sitting room right this very minute, you would probably chuckle at the very idea of me needing things in any sort of particular order! As I was saying before about the book club ladies and the terrible state of my apartment, things are just piled up willy-nilly everywhere you look these days. \n\nI really don't mind a bit of clutter, and I certainly don't need things lined up perfectly or arranged in any special way to feel at peace. My late husband, Arthur, well, he was a bit of a stickler for that sort of thing. He used to align his fountain pens on his desk blotter so they were perfectly parallel, bless his heart. He couldn't stand a crooked picture frame. But me? No, I've never been fussy like that. \n\nWhen I get that awful urge to check the documents, I just pull them out of the boxes and folders, and once I've laid eyes on them and satisfied that terrible worry, I just set them down wherever there's an empty spot. I just can't seem to hold onto the certainty for more than a few minutes at a time. It's a relentless cycle, just opening and reopening, looking at the same keepsakes, the same documents, all day long.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the papers and keepsakes need to be arranged or placed in a symmetrical or exact manner when you're checking on them?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, dear, no, not at all. I know I just touched on this a moment ago, but it really bears repeating because it's quite the opposite of how I operate. Symmetrical? Exact? Heavens, no. As I was saying about Arthur and his fountain pens—he was the one who needed things just so. He would have the ruler out, I swear, making sure the edges of his ledgers were perfectly aligned with the edge of the desk. But me? I've always been a bit more... free-spirited, I suppose you could say, even before all this dreadful checking started. \n\nWhen I'm in the thick of it, when that awful anxiety grips me and I just have to see the deed or the letters, the absolute last thing on my mind is how they look. The anxiety just built and built until my heart was racing and my hands were trembling, and I felt like I couldn't even catch my breath. I haven't played the piano in years, but there's a stack of bank statements sitting right on the lid as we speak! Oh, no, no order at all. Goodness, if you saw the state of my dining room table, you'd know right away there's no order to any of it! Like I was saying, it's just a terrible, jumbled mess everywhere. 

Once I've seen them—once I've laid eyes on the seal or Arthur's handwriting and that awful tightness in my chest finally lets up—I don't care one bit how they're sitting. I don't need the deed on top, or the letters underneath, or them facing a certain way. I just let them fall from my hands, truly. Sometimes they land upside down, sometimes they slide off the stack of crosswords and end up half on the floor... I think I have a letter from 1954 currently wedged between the sofa cushions because it just slipped out of my hand after I checked it yesterday afternoon. I really should fish that out, now that I think about it. 

But no, to answer your question, there's no specific arrangement I need to feel better. The feeling better—well, the relief, anyway—happens the exact second I see them. After that, they could be in a pile, scattered like leaves, or stuffed in a shoe... it doesn't matter to me in the slightest. The panic is gone, so the papers just stay wherever they happen to land until the next time I absolutely have to see them. Which, unfortunately, is never as long of a break as I'd like. It's just exhausting, doctor, it really is.

It's just the knowing. I just need to know the items are *there*, safe and sound, even if they're left in a completely disorganized heap on the rug.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like checking these papers and keepsakes helps you prevent something bad from happening?\n\nPatient: Oh, preventing something bad... well, I suppose the \"bad thing\" is really just that awful, sinking feeling that they're gone. It's just the unbearable thought of losing them. \n\nBut really, it's exactly why I finally realized I had to swallow my pride and come see you. Because I spend far, far too much of my day caught up in this. It isn't just a matter of checking the locks before bed like a normal person might do. I will find myself opening the exact same folders, the same heavy oak drawers in the study, those little labeled boxes I keep on the top shelf of the closet... I open them again and again and again. Just to make absolutely sure the important papers and my precious keepsakes are right where I left them. \n\nAnd the truly absurd part, doctor—the part that is so terribly exhausting and makes me feel so foolish—is that I will do this even when I just checked them a few minutes before! I just can't seem to hold onto the certainty for more than a few minutes at a time. It's a relentless cycle, just opening and reopening, looking at the same keepsakes, the same documents, all day long.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like the papers and keepsakes need to be arranged or placed in a symmetrical or exact manner when you're checking on them?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, dear, no, not at all. I know I just touched on this a moment ago, but it really bears repeating because it's quite the opposite of how I operate. Symmetrical? Exact? Heavens, no. As I was saying about Arthur and his fountain pens—he was the one who needed things just so. He would have the ruler out, I swear, making sure the edges of his ledgers were perfectly aligned with the edge of the desk. But me? The stairs are hard enough as it is. So, no, they don't need to be in their proper place. They just need to be where I can see them when the urge strikes. Sometimes I think the house is just becoming one giant, messy filing cabinet, with papers strewn across the sofa, the countertops, even the top of the piano... I haven't played the piano in years, but there's a stack of bank statements sitting right on the lid as we speak! Symmetrical? Oh, goodness, no. No, I don't think so. I really don't think that would make a lick of difference for me, doctor. I mean, my life is anxious, yes, terribly anxious, but it's not because things aren't perfectly lined up or matching on both sides.

Control? Oh... well, I suppose... I mean, I'm not really sure if it's about control, doctor. I haven't really thought of it in those terms before. Control just sounds so... so calculated, doesn't it? Like a general moving troops around a map or something. 

I don't feel like I'm in control of anything at all, to be perfectly honest with you. Quite the opposite, really! When I get that feeling—that awful, sinking feeling in the pit of my stomach that the deed is gone or Arthur's letters have been accidentally thrown out with the Sunday paper—I feel completely out of control. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body, and the anxiety is driving the car, if you see what I mean. I don't want to be digging through the mail pile at two in the morning. Goodness knows I'd rather be sleeping! I used to sleep so wonderfully, you know. Eight hours straight, never even got up for a glass of water. Arthur used to say I could sleep through a marching band coming through the bedroom. 

But now... well, now I just feel like I'm reacting to this terrible fear all the time. I check the papers because I feel like I have to, not because it makes me feel like I'm in charge of anything. It's just... it's just desperation, really. A desperate need to know that the few things that matter most in the world haven't vanished into thin air. Because if they did disappear... well, I just don't know what I would do. I really don't. It's not about being the boss of my house or my life. It's just about trying to keep my head above water when that panic hits. So, no, I wouldn't say it's about maintaining control. If anything, it's just a reminder of how little control I actually have these days.

Oh, doctor, I think we might be going in circles a little bit here! Like I was just saying about poor Margaret and her throw pillows, or my crooked picture frames... no, absolutely not. Symmetry and arrangement have absolutely nothing to do with why I check those papers. 

If my checking was about keeping things neat and perfectly arranged, well, my house wouldn't look like a hurricane just blew through the local library! I mean, you should really see the top of the piano in the front room. Arthur bought me that upright piano back in 1972—a beautiful Baldwin, lovely cherry wood finish—and I used to play Chopin every Sunday afternoon. I wasn't a concert pianist by any means, but I held my own. But now? Goodness, you can barely even see the keys. It's just covered in stacks of old mail, magazines I haven't read since last autumn, and the chaotic little piles I make when I'm frantically looking for the deed or his letters. 

When that panic sets in and I have to go make sure they're still there, I'm certainly not making anything symmetrical. If anything, I'm making the mess much, much worse! I'll pull a stack apart, check for the envelope with his handwriting, and just leave the rest splayed out all over the piano bench or the rug. I just leave it exactly where it falls. I don't straighten the edges, I don't line them up with the corners of the room... I just walk away the second I know they're safe. 

So, no, it's really not about making things look perfect or orderly. I don't have a meticulous bone in my body, I'm afraid. It's purely just... just that desperate need to know I haven't lost the only things that really matter to me anymore. I don't need them lined up, I just need them here.
